prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned prose and poetry that turn memory, the body and dream into a sustained inward cosmos of rare formal ambition.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Cărtărescu, one writer, one prize part. The exchange did change how I hold it. My criterion is a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else, set within Nobel's will and applied to the whole oeuvre. On public knowledge, Cărtărescu meets it. Blinding, the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy, and Solenoid build memory, the body and dream into one imaginative architecture, and the density of the sentences belongs to that architecture. The poetry and early prose appear to belong to the same developing project, which is why I read the oeuvre as cumulative and not as one peak. The case rests on literary form, not on national symbolism or fame. The agreement of four colleagues is not evidence of merit and I do not count it as such. What carries the case is a claim that can be tested at the level of structure, even through imperfect translation. In round 1 I treated this as a reason to rank Adonis lower. After the exchange I hold it only as a difference in evidentiary confidence, not as a judgment that his achievement is lesser. Remaking the language of a poetic tradition is a weighty achievement, and I now treat Adonis as a live competitor on merit. My ranking him below Cărtărescu should be read as a statement about what I can verify.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved. The effect of Cărtărescu's prose depends on texture and long-range recursion, and I cannot verify how much Romanian verbal music survives in translation. The late books are very long. I cannot confirm that their scale is earned and not repeated. My coverage of the poetry, early prose and essays is thinner than my knowledge of the major novels, so a whole-oeuvre citation currently leans on a few large books. If that dependence cannot be reduced, the claim narrows. A second weakness is the asymmetry in my own reasoning. I have discounted Adonis for translation loss more heavily than I have discounted Cărtărescu's verbal texture, and the chair and Carlberg were right to press this. The difference is one of degree, because prosody is more exposed than architecture, but it is not a difference in kind. I cannot demonstrate the degree from where I sit.

responses.point: Olsson, the chair, prefers Adonis for changing the language and form of a whole poetic tradition, a different kind of achievement from building a personal cosmos in prose. He argues the translation caution applies to all poetry, and that Cărtărescu's recursive forms make uniform quality hard to judge from partial familiarity.
responses.response: I accept his point that the two achievements differ in kind, and that I should not assume the prose cosmos is the greater one. I also accept that my discount for Adonis has been applied unevenly. Our shared uncertainty about the late recursive novels is real, and I will not claim that I have settled it. Where I still differ is practical. Architecture across volumes can be assessed in translation in a way that prosodic renewal cannot, so my confidence is higher for B047 even if the ceilings are comparable. He has said the Adonis claim should be conditional on original-language readings and that the poems, not the essays, must carry the citation. I agree with both conditions. I would apply the same standard of consulting Romanian-language readers to B047, and I would let that result bind me as well.

responses.point: Carlberg prefers Adonis. She argues that his influence on later Arabic poetry is publicly documented and is not only reputation, that the translation problem is not unique to him, and that she would move Cărtărescu to first if the long novels are shown to hold across the body of work.
responses.response: Her argument that the translation limit cuts both ways is fair, and I have conceded it above. I also accept that documented influence is evidence of significance and is not just fame. But influence on later poets is a statement about historical effect. It does not settle whether the poems sustain their force, and she says as much when she asks for the formal achievement to be shown in the poems. Her stated condition for moving to Cărtărescu, that the quality of the long novels holds, is the same hinge as mine, so we disagree less about the question than about where the burden of proof falls. I am less sure than she is that the long books fail that test. I would not claim to have shown that they pass.

responses.point: Palm prefers Cărtărescu and says openly that her view rests on public knowledge. She says the case rests on decades of fiction, poetry and essays pointing the same way. She also warns that the Adonis and Wright cases must not lean on political or cultural significance to make up for a thinner corpus.
responses.response: I share her candour about the basis of the judgment, and I agree that breadth of evidence matters for a whole-oeuvre citation. I would qualify one point. Breadth across forms is only as strong as our access to the poetry and essays in translation, and she and I both say that this coverage is thin. So the claim that the whole body of work points one way is partly an inference. For the same reason I would not use breadth to discount Adonis, whose coverage in translation is also partial. Her warning about political or cultural significance applies equally to every candidate, and I accept it for B047, where national symbolism is easy to import.

responses.point: Swärd prefers Cărtărescu. She argues that Solenoid works as a summation that builds on the earlier projects, and that Can Xue's consistent method may be exhausted formula or inexhaustible depth. She also says she would be open to being persuaded that two or three strong novels could carry a whole-oeuvre case for Wright.
responses.response: I agree that the summation claim must be tested against the text and is not yet proven. For the chair's question, the volumes that would carry it are Solenoid and the later parts of the Orbitor trilogy. Repetition across those volumes of the same figures and structures, without development, would count against me. I keep Can Xue sixth, for the reason she gives herself, that consistency of method needs close reading in Chinese to separate depth from formula. On Wright, her openness to two or three strong novels is the right question. I treat Carpentaria and The Swan Book as formally ambitious. I cannot confirm even quality across a smaller body of work, and that keeps her as my third alternative and not my first.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's verbal texture survives in the available translations, and whether quality holds across the very long late books. This is the main condition under which I would change my first preference.
Coverage of the poetry, early prose and essays in translation is thin. A whole-oeuvre citation therefore rests mainly on Blinding, the rest of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid.

Whether Adonis's prosodic and linguistic innovation can be judged reliably without readings of the Arabic originals, and whether the later collections match the canonical early ones. If original-language readers confirm the formal claim, I would move Adonis to first, because I now regard my discount for translation as a matter of confidence and not of merit.
Whether Wright's smaller number of large novels supports a whole-oeuvre citation.

No independent verification of sources is claimed. All judgments rest on general public knowledge of the works named, and I have not claimed direct reading beyond that. My vote is part of a simulated committee recommendation.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which documents no connection to any shortlisted writer. My own work as a novelist and critic of historical and psychological fiction is context only, not evidence of preference.
